title: Introduction to Lumenex Indexes
body:
## Overview

An **index** in Lumenex is a logical collection of JSON documents that share a common mapping and configuration. Every document is assigned to exactly one index, and every search request targets one or more indexes. If you are coming from a relational database, an index is roughly analogous to a table, although the comparison breaks down when you consider schema flexibility and distributed storage.

Each index is split into one or more **shards**. A shard is a self-contained search unit that holds a subset of the index's documents. Shards may have **replicas**, which are read-only copies that improve fault tolerance and search throughput.

## Core Concepts

- **Document**: a JSON object identified by a unique `_id` within its index.
- **Field**: a named value inside a document, typed through the index mapping.
- **Primary shard**: a horizontal partition of an index. The primary shard count is fixed at creation time.
- **Replica shard**: a copy of a primary shard. The replica count can be changed at any time.

## Creating Your First Index

The simplest way to create an index is to send a `PUT` request with no body:

```bash
curl -X PUT 'http://localhost:9200/products'
```

This creates the `products` index with default settings: one primary shard and one replica. Lumenex also infers a mapping from the first document you index, unless dynamic mapping has been disabled.

## Inspecting an Index

Use the `_cat` endpoint to review the index at a glance:

```bash
curl 'http://localhost:9200/_cat/indices/products?v'
```

The output lists health, document count, store size, and shard configuration. For detailed settings, query the `_settings` endpoint instead.

## Naming Rules

Index names must be lowercase, must not start with an underscore, and must not contain spaces, commas, or the characters `/ * ? < > |`. Names are limited to 255 bytes.

> **Note:** Index names are immutable. To rename an index, create a new one and reindex the data, or use an alias so that client code is decoupled from the physical name.

## Best Practices

- Prefer descriptive, lowercase names that include the data domain, such as `orders-2024`.
- Avoid creating thousands of small indexes, since each index carries fixed overhead in cluster state.
- Plan primary shard counts before ingestion begins. Changing them later requires a split or reindex operation.

title: Index Settings and Creation Options
body:
## Overview

Index settings control how Lumenex stores, distributes, and refreshes data. Some settings can be changed on a live index, while others are fixed when the index is created. This page describes the options you are most likely to set at creation time and explains which ones are dynamic.

## Creating an Index with Settings

Settings are supplied in the request body of a `PUT` call. The following example creates an index with three primary shards, one replica, and a one-second refresh interval:

```json
{
  "settings": {
    "number_of_shards": 3,
    "number_of_replicas": 1,
    "refresh_interval": "1s"
  }
}
```

Send the body with:

```bash
curl -X PUT 'http://localhost:9200/orders' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @orders-index.json
```

## Static and Dynamic Settings

| Setting | Type | Changeable After Creation |
|---|---|---|
| `number_of_shards` | Static | No |
| `number_of_replicas` | Dynamic | Yes |
| `refresh_interval` | Dynamic | Yes |
| `codec` | Static | No |

Static settings are baked into the on-disk structure of the index. Dynamic settings can be updated with a `PUT` to the `_settings` endpoint.

## Choosing a Shard Count

A useful starting point is to aim for shard sizes between 10 GB and 50 GB. Too many small shards increase cluster state size and per-query overhead, while a few oversized shards slow recovery and rebalancing. Remember that the primary shard count cannot be changed without a split or reindex.

## Refresh Interval Tuning

The `refresh_interval` setting determines how often newly indexed documents become visible to search. Setting it to `-1` disables automatic refresh, which is useful during large bulk loads.

> **Warning:** If you disable refresh during ingestion, remember to restore the interval afterwards. Documents remain unsearchable until a manual refresh or the restored interval occurs.

## Replica Strategy

Replicas can be increased during peak read periods and reduced during maintenance windows. Setting `number_of_replicas` to `0` removes redundancy and should be done only on indexes that can be rebuilt from a source of truth.

## Validation

Lumenex rejects unknown setting keys with a 400 response. Always verify your configuration after creation by calling `GET /orders/_settings` and confirming the values returned.

title: Field Data Types
body:
## Overview

A field's data type determines how its values are stored, indexed, and queried. Lumenex supports scalar types, structured types, and specialized types for geospatial and vector data. Choosing the correct type at mapping time is one of the most important decisions you will make, because changing a field's type later generally requires reindexing.

## Commonly Used Types

| Type | Use Case | Example Value |
|---|---|---|
| `keyword` | Exact matching, filtering, aggregations | `"SKU-10293"` |
| `text` | Full-text search with analysis | `"waterproof hiking boot"` |
| `integer` / `long` | Whole numbers | `42` |
| `float` / `scaled_float` | Decimal measurements | `19.99` |
| `date` | Timestamps and dates | `"2024-05-14T08:30:00Z"` |
| `boolean` | Flags | `true` |
| `geo_point` | Latitude and longitude | `{"lat": 51.5, "lon": -0.12}` |

## Declaring Field Types

Fields are declared under the `properties` key of a mapping:

```json
{
  "mappings": {
    "properties": {
      "sku": { "type": "keyword" },
      "title": { "type": "text" },
      "price": { "type": "scaled_float", "scaling_factor": 100 },
      "released_at": { "type": "date" }
    }
  }
}
```

## Text Versus Keyword

A common mistake is mapping every string as `text`. Text fields are analyzed into tokens, so they support relevance-ranked full-text queries but cannot be sorted or aggregated efficiently. Keyword fields store the raw value and are ideal for identifiers, tags, and categories. Multi-fields let you index the same source value both ways:

```json
"title": {
  "type": "text",
  "fields": { "raw": { "type": "keyword" } }
}
```

## Numeric Precision

Use `scaled_float` for monetary values to avoid floating-point rounding. The stored value is multiplied by the scaling factor and kept as a long.

## Structured Types

Objects and nested fields allow hierarchical documents. Use `nested` only when you need to query array elements independently, since nested documents carry additional indexing cost.

> **Note:** Once a field has been mapped, its type cannot be changed in place. Adding a new field is always allowed, but altering an existing one requires creating a new index and reindexing.

## Summary

Choose types deliberately, use multi-fields when a value must serve both search and filtering, and document your mapping decisions alongside your application code.

Bulk Indexing API
body:
## Overview

The Bulk API lets you index, update, or delete many documents in a single HTTP request. Sending documents one at a time incurs network latency and per-request overhead for every record, so bulk requests are the recommended approach for ingestion pipelines, backfills, and batch synchronization jobs.

## Request Format

Bulk requests use newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON). Each action line is followed, where applicable, by a source line. Every line must end with a newline character, including the last one.

```json
{"index": {"_index": "orders", "_id": "1001"}}
{"customer_id": "C-88", "total": 129.50, "status": "paid"}
{"delete": {"_index": "orders", "_id": "1000"}}
{"update": {"_index": "orders", "_id": "999"}}
{"doc": {"status": "shipped"}}
```

Send the file with:

```bash
curl -X POST 'http://localhost:9200/_bulk' -H 'Content-Type: application/x-ndjson' --data-binary @batch.ndjson
```

## Supported Actions

- `index`: creates a document or replaces an existing one with the same `_id`.
- `create`: fails if a document with the same `_id` already exists.
- `update`: applies a partial document or script to an existing document.
- `delete`: removes a document by `_id`.

## Choosing a Batch Size

A common starting point is 5 to 15 MB per request, or 1,000 to 5,000 documents, depending on document size. Benchmark your own workload. Very large requests can exhaust heap memory on coordinating nodes, while very small ones waste throughput.

## Interpreting Responses

A bulk request returns HTTP 200 even when individual actions fail. Always check the top-level `errors` boolean and inspect each item's `status` code. Failed items should be retried with exponential backoff or written to a dead-letter index for review.

## Performance Tips

- Use multiple worker threads, but cap concurrency to avoid rejected-execution errors.
- Temporarily set `refresh_interval` to `-1` during large backfills, then restore it.
- Set `number_of_replicas` to `0` during the initial load and add replicas afterwards.

> **Warning:** Bulk requests are not transactional. If a request fails midway, some actions may have succeeded and others may not. Design idempotent pipelines by supplying explicit `_id` values so retries overwrite rather than duplicate documents.

## Summary

Batch your writes, validate every response item, and use stable document identifiers so that ingestion remains safe to retry.

title: Reindexing and Index Aliases
body:
## Overview

Reindexing copies documents from a source index into a destination index, applying a new mapping, new settings, or a transformation along the way. Combined with **index aliases**, reindexing allows you to change the physical structure of your data without requiring application downtime. This page describes both techniques and how to use them together.

## When to Reindex

You need to reindex when you must change a field's type, alter an analyzer, change the primary shard count, or migrate to a new major mapping version. These changes cannot be applied in place to existing documents.

## Running a Reindex

The `_reindex` API reads from a source and writes to a destination:

```json
{
  "source": { "index": "orders-v1" },
  "dest": { "index": "orders-v2" },
  "script": {
    "lang": "painless",
    "source": "ctx._source.total_cents = (long)(ctx._source.total * 100)"
  }
}
```

Submit the request with:

```bash
curl -X POST 'http://localhost:9200/_reindex?wait_for_completion=false' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @reindex.json
```

Setting `wait_for_completion=false` returns a task identifier, which you can poll through the `_tasks` endpoint.

## Index Aliases

An alias is a named pointer to one or more indexes. Applications query the alias rather than the physical index, so the underlying index can be swapped atomically:

```json
{
  "actions": [
    { "remove": { "index": "orders-v1", "alias": "orders" } },
    { "add": { "index": "orders-v2", "alias": "orders" } }
  ]
}
```

Both actions in the `actions` array are applied as a single atomic operation, so queries never see a moment when the alias points to nothing.

## Zero-Downtime Migration Procedure

1. Create the new index with the desired mapping.
2. Run `_reindex` from the old index to the new one.
3. Dual-write new changes to both indexes, or repeat the reindex for recent data.
4. Verify document counts and sample query results.
5. Atomically switch the alias.
6. Retain the old index briefly for rollback, then delete it.

> **Warning:** Deleting the source index before verifying the destination is a frequent cause of data loss. Keep the old index until the new one has been validated under production traffic.

## Filtering Documents During Reindex

The `query` field inside `source` limits which documents are copied. This is useful for incremental migrations, where you copy only documents updated after a given timestamp.

## Summary

Use aliases for every application-facing index, reindex with task monitoring, and treat the alias switch as the single point of cutover.

VectorForge Configuration Guide: Getting Started
body:
# Getting Started with VectorForge Configuration

This guide explains how to configure VectorForge, a fictional vector search and embeddings engine, for production workloads. Read this page first. Later sections assume you understand the concepts introduced here.

## Core Concepts

VectorForge stores **collections**. Each collection holds **records**, and each record contains a dense vector, an optional sparse vector, and a JSON metadata object. A collection is configured once at creation time through a configuration file. Some settings can be changed later, while others are locked after the first insert.

The configuration is organized into five top-level blocks:

- `embedding`: the model and dimensionality used to produce vectors
- `index`: the approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) structure
- `metric`: the similarity function used to rank results
- `storage`: quantization and on-disk layout
- `cluster`: sharding and replication

## A Minimal Configuration

```yaml
collection: product_catalog
embedding:
  dimensions: 768
  normalize: true
index:
  type: hnsw
  ef_construction: 200
  m: 16
metric: cosine
storage:
  quantization: none
cluster:
  shards: 1
  replicas: 1
```

This configuration creates a single-shard collection that stores full-precision 768-dimensional vectors and ranks results by cosine similarity.

## Validating Your Configuration

Run the validator before deploying any change:

```
vforge config validate --file product_catalog.yaml
```

The validator checks type constraints, verifies that the metric is compatible with the chosen embedding normalization, and warns about combinations that are known to degrade recall.

## Recommended Workflow

1. Define the embedding model and dimensions.
2. Choose a metric that matches how the model was trained.
3. Select an index type and tune its build parameters.
4. Add quantization only after measuring recall on a representative sample.
5. Plan sharding once you know your expected record count and query rate.

> **Warning:** The `embedding.dimensions` and `metric` fields are immutable after the first record is written. Changing them requires creating a new collection and re-ingesting all data. Validate these two fields carefully before inserting production data.

## Next Steps

Continue to the Index Configuration section to learn how HNSW parameters affect the balance between recall, latency, and memory use.

title: HNSW Index Parameters and Trade-offs
body:
# HNSW Index Parameters and Trade-offs

VectorForge uses a Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graph as its default approximate nearest neighbor index. This page describes each tunable parameter and explains how changing it affects recall, build time, query latency, and memory consumption.

## Parameter Overview

HNSW exposes three build-time parameters and one query-time parameter.

| Parameter | Scope | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `m` | Build | 16 | Maximum number of bidirectional links per node |
| `ef_construction` | Build | 200 | Candidate list size during graph construction |
| `ef_search` | Query | 64 | Candidate list size during each query |
| `max_layers` | Build | auto | Upper bound on hierarchy depth |

Build-time parameters are fixed once the index is created. The `ef_search` value can be adjusted per query.

## Choosing `m`

A higher `m` improves recall on high-dimensional data but increases memory use roughly in proportion to `m`. For most embedding workloads between 384 and 1024 dimensions, values between 12 and 32 perform well. Values above 48 rarely help and substantially increase index size.

## Choosing `ef_construction`

This parameter controls how thoroughly the graph is built. Doubling it roughly doubles build time but usually yields a modest recall gain. Set it to at least `2 * m`.

## Tuning `ef_search`

The query-time parameter is the most useful lever for operators. Increase `ef_search` when recall is too low and reduce it when latency is too high.

```yaml
index:
  type: hnsw
  m: 24
  ef_construction: 300
query_defaults:
  ef_search: 96
```

You can also override the value for a single request:

```
search --collection product_catalog --k 10 --ef_search 128 --vector @query.bin
```

## Memory Estimation

Approximate index memory in bytes can be estimated as:

```
nodes * (dimensions * 4 + m * 2 * 8)
```

This excludes metadata and the write-ahead log. For a collection of 10 million 768-dimensional vectors with `m` set to 16, expect roughly 35 to 45 GB of index memory before quantization.

## Measuring Recall

Always measure recall against a brute-force baseline on a sample of queries. The `vforge bench recall` command performs this comparison and reports recall at k for several `ef_search` values.

> **Note:** Recall measurements are only meaningful when the baseline uses the same metric and the same normalization as the index. Mismatched settings produce misleadingly high or low recall figures.

## Summary

Start with the defaults, measure recall on real queries, and adjust `ef_search` first. Change `m` or `ef_construction` only when query-time tuning cannot reach your recall target, because those changes require a full rebuild.

title: Embedding Pipeline Configuration
body:
# Embedding Pipeline Configuration

VectorForge can generate embeddings internally or accept precomputed vectors from your application. This page describes how to configure the built-in embedding pipeline, how to register external models, and how to keep embeddings consistent across ingestion and query time.

## Operating Modes

The engine supports three modes:

- **Precomputed**: Clients send vectors directly. VectorForge performs no transformation other than optional normalization.
- **Managed**: VectorForge calls a registered model to embed raw text or images at ingestion and query time.
- **Hybrid**: Documents are embedded by the engine, while queries are embedded by the client using the same model.

Hybrid mode is the most error-prone. If the query model differs in any way from the document model, similarity scores become meaningless.

## Registering a Model

Models are registered in the `embedding` block. Each registration includes a model identifier, a revision pin, and the expected output dimensions.

```yaml
embedding:
  mode: managed
  model: vf-embed-base
  revision: 2024-11-03
  dimensions: 768
  input_field: description
  batch_size: 64
  normalize: true
  max_input_tokens: 512
```

Always pin a revision. Unpinned models can change behavior when the provider publishes an update, which silently breaks compatibility with previously stored vectors.

## Batching and Throughput

The `batch_size` setting determines how many inputs are sent to the model in one call. Larger batches improve throughput on GPU-backed inference but increase peak memory. Start with 32 and increase until GPU utilization plateaus.

## Normalization

When `normalize` is true, every vector is scaled to unit length before storage. This is required when you use cosine similarity with dot-product indexing, and it is recommended in most other cases. Normalization happens after model output and before quantization.

## Handling Long Inputs

Inputs longer than `max_input_tokens` are truncated by default. You can change this behavior:

```yaml
embedding:
  truncation: chunk
  chunk_overlap: 32
```

With `chunk` enabled, each long document produces multiple vectors, each linked to the same parent record ID. Search results are deduplicated by parent ID before being returned.

## Consistency Checks

Each stored vector carries a fingerprint of the model name, revision, and normalization setting. At query time, VectorForge compares the fingerprint of the query embedding with the collection's fingerprint and rejects mismatches.

> **Warning:** Disabling fingerprint checks with `consistency.enforce: false` allows queries embedded with a different model to run without error. Results will look plausible but will be ranked essentially at random. Keep enforcement enabled in all production environments.

## Migrating to a New Model

To change models, create a new collection, set the new revision, and re-embed all source documents. Old and new collections can be queried side by side during cutover using the alias feature described in the operations guide.

title: Distance Metrics and Similarity Scoring
body:
# Distance Metrics and Similarity Scoring

The `metric` setting determines how VectorForge measures closeness between vectors. Choosing the wrong metric is one of the most common causes of poor search quality, and it is difficult to detect because results still appear reasonable. This page explains the supported metrics and when to use each.

## Supported Metrics

| Metric | Identifier | Range | Higher means |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cosine similarity | `cosine` | -1 to 1 | More similar |
| Dot product | `dot` | Unbounded | More similar |
| Euclidean distance | `l2` | 0 to infinity | Less similar |
| Hamming distance | `hamming` | 0 to dimensions | Less similar (binary vectors only) |

VectorForge reports scores in a consistent direction for every metric in the API response, so client code that sorts by `score` does not need to know which metric is active. Internally, `l2` and `hamming` are converted to negated distances.

## Matching the Metric to the Model

Embedding models are trained with a specific objective. Use the metric recommended in the model card. In general:

- Models trained with contrastive loss on cosine similarity should use `cosine`.
- Models that output normalized vectors can use `dot` for slightly faster search, because dot product on unit vectors is equivalent to cosine similarity.
- Models that encode magnitude as meaningful information should use `l2`.

## Configuration Example

```yaml
metric: dot
embedding:
  normalize: true
```

The validator will reject this combination if normalization is disabled, because dot product on unnormalized vectors produces scores dominated by vector length.

## Score Thresholds

You can require a minimum score for returned results:

```
search --collection product_catalog --k 20 --min_score 0.72 --vector @query.bin
```

Thresholds are metric-specific. A cosine threshold of 0.72 has no meaningful relationship to an L2 threshold of 0.72. When you change metrics, recalibrate every threshold against a labeled evaluation set.

## Binary Vectors

When `storage.quantization` is set to `binary`, the metric is forced to `hamming`. Hamming distance on binary codes is extremely fast but less precise. It is best used as a first-stage candidate generator followed by rescoring with full-precision vectors.

```yaml
storage:
  quantization: binary
  rescore: true
  rescore_multiplier: 4
```

## Common Mistakes

- Using `l2` with normalized embeddings. This is mathematically related to cosine but produces different rankings when vectors have unequal norms, which can happen after pipeline changes.
- Forgetting that `cosine` in VectorForge internally normalizes vectors. Adding your own normalization is harmless but unnecessary.

> **Note:** The metric is stored with the collection and cannot be changed in place. A metric change requires re-indexing, and it is the same operation as creating a new collection described in the Getting Started guide.

title: Quantization for Storage Optimization
body:
# Quantization for Storage Optimization

Full-precision float32 vectors consume four bytes per dimension. For large collections, this dominates memory and disk costs. VectorForge supports several quantization schemes that trade a controlled amount of accuracy for significant reductions in storage and bandwidth. This page describes each option and how to evaluate it.

## Quantization Options

| Scheme | Identifier | Bytes per dimension | Typical recall loss |
|---|---|---|---|
| None | `none` | 4.0 | 0 |
| Scalar 8-bit | `sq8` | 1.0 | Under 1 percent |
| Scalar 4-bit | `sq4` | 0.5 | 1 to 3 percent |
| Product quantization | `pq` | Configurable | 2 to 8 percent |
| Binary | `binary` | 0.125 | 5 to 15 percent without rescoring |

The recall figures above are typical for normalized embeddings and will vary with your data. Always measure them.

## Scalar Quantization

Scalar quantization maps each float to a fixed-width integer using per-dimension minimum and maximum values learned during indexing. The `sq8` scheme is the safest first step.

```yaml
storage:
  quantization: sq8
  keep_originals: false
  training_sample: 100000
```

The `training_sample` setting controls how many vectors are used to learn the value ranges. Use at least 50,000 vectors for stable estimates.

## Product Quantization

Product quantization splits each vector into subvectors and encodes each with a codebook. It achieves the smallest footprint for high-dimensional data but requires careful tuning.

```yaml
storage:
  quantization: pq
  pq_subvectors: 96
  pq_bits: 8
  rescore: true
  rescore_multiplier: 3
```

The number of subvectors must divide the dimensionality evenly. For 768 dimensions, valid choices include 96, 128, 192, and 256.

## Rescoring

Rescoring retrieves a larger candidate set using compressed vectors, then recomputes exact scores using stored originals. The `rescore_multiplier` determines how many extra candidates are fetched. A value of 3 means that for `k = 10`, the engine fetches 30 candidates and rescores them.

Rescoring requires that originals remain on disk. Setting `keep_originals: false` disables it.

## Measuring the Impact

Run a recall comparison before enabling quantization in production:

```
vforge bench recall --collection product_catalog --baseline none --candidate sq8 --queries 2000 --k 10
```

The report includes recall at k, median latency, and index size for each configuration.

> **Warning:** Quantization parameters are learned from the data present at index build time. If your data distribution shifts significantly after deployment, for example when a new product category is added, recall can degrade without any error. Schedule periodic recall checks and retrain quantization when the drop exceeds your threshold.

## Recommendation

For most collections under 50 million vectors, `sq8` with rescoring provides a good balance. Move to `pq` only when memory constraints make `sq8` infeasible, and always keep rescoring enabled with `pq`.

title: Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Queries
body:
# Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Queries

Most real search applications combine vector similarity with structured constraints, such as price ranges, categories, or availability. VectorForge supports metadata filters that are applied during ANN traversal rather than as a post-processing step. This page explains how to declare filterable fields and how filter selectivity affects performance.

## Declaring Filterable Fields

Only fields declared in the `filters` block can be used in query predicates. Declaring fields increases ingestion cost, so include only those you actually filter on.

```yaml
filters:
  fields:
    - name: category
      type: keyword
    - name: price
      type: float
    - name: in_stock
      type: boolean
    - name: created_at
      type: timestamp
```

Supported types are `keyword`, `integer`, `float`, `boolean`, and `timestamp`. Text fields are not filterable and should be handled through the optional lexical search component instead.

## Filter Strategies

VectorForge chooses one of two execution strategies for each query:

- **Pre-filter**: The engine computes the set of matching record IDs first, then searches only within that set. This is efficient when the filter is highly selective, meaning it matches a small fraction of records.
- **In-graph filter**: The engine traverses the HNSW graph and skips non-matching nodes during search. This is efficient when the filter matches a large fraction of records.

The planner switches between strategies based on estimated selectivity. You can override it:

```yaml
query_defaults:
  filter_strategy: auto
  selectivity_threshold: 0.05
```

Setting `selectivity_threshold` to 0.05 means filters matching fewer than 5 percent of records use pre-filtering.

## Example Query

```
search --collection product_catalog --k 10 --ef_search 96 \
  --filter 'category == "footwear" AND price < 120 AND in_stock == true' \
  --vector @query.bin
```

## Recall Under Filtering

Restrictive filters can reduce recall in graph-based search because the graph may become disconnected within the filtered subset. To compensate, the engine automatically increases the effective `ef_search` when selectivity is low. You can set a floor:

```yaml
query_defaults:
  min_ef_search: 128
```

## Hybrid Scoring

When lexical search is enabled, results from vector and keyword retrieval are merged using reciprocal rank fusion. The `hybrid.weight` parameter controls how much each source contributes, with 0 meaning pure lexical and 1 meaning pure vector.

> **Note:** Hybrid scoring requires that the `text` field be indexed separately. It does not change how metadata filters are applied, so filters apply equally to both retrieval paths.

## Common Pitfalls

- Filtering on a field that was not declared results in a validation error at query time, not at ingestion. Check your `filters` block before deploying a new client.
- Timestamp filters must use UTC. Local-time strings are accepted but silently converted using the server time zone.

> **Warning:** Filters on `keyword` fields are case-sensitive. A query for `Footwear` will not match records stored as `footwear`. Normalize values during ingestion to avoid empty result sets.

title: Sharding and Replication Configuration
body:
# Sharding and Replication Configuration

A single VectorForge node can serve collections of tens of millions of vectors, but larger workloads require distribution across multiple shards and replicas. This page describes how records are partitioned, how replicas maintain consistency, and how to size a cluster for your workload.

## Concepts

- **Shard**: A partition of a collection. Each record belongs to exactly one shard, determined by a hash of its primary key.
- **Replica**: A copy of a shard. Replicas serve reads and provide failover.
- **Node**: A process that hosts one or more shard replicas.

Queries are fanned out to one replica per shard. The coordinator merges the top results from each shard into a global top k.

## Basic Configuration

```yaml
cluster:
  shards: 4
  replicas: 2
  placement: spread
  write_consistency: quorum
  read_consistency: one
```

This configuration creates eight shard replicas. With `spread` placement, the engine avoids putting two replicas of the same shard on the same node or availability zone.

## Choosing the Shard Count

Shard count is fixed at collection creation. Choose it based on expected final size rather than current size. A useful guideline is to keep each shard below 20 million vectors for latency-sensitive workloads. Too many shards increases fan-out overhead, because every query touches every shard. For collections under 5 million vectors, one or two shards are usually sufficient.

## Replication and Consistency

Writes are acknowledged when the configured `write_consistency` is satisfied:

- `one`: Acknowledged after one replica confirms. Fastest, but a node failure can lose recent writes.
- `quorum`: Acknowledged after a majority of replicas confirm. Recommended for most deployments.
- `all`: Acknowledged after every replica confirms. Strongest guarantee, lowest write availability.

Reads use `read_consistency` in a similar way. Reading at `one` is usually acceptable for search, because slight staleness rarely affects ranking quality.

## Rebalancing

When you add nodes, run the rebalance command to move shard replicas and balance load:

```
vforge cluster rebalance --collection product_catalog --max_concurrent_moves 2
```

Rebalancing copies index segments and does not block reads, but it temporarily increases network and disk usage. Limit concurrent moves on production clusters.

## Sizing Example

Suppose you expect 60 million 768-dimensional vectors with sq8 quantization and a target of 2,000 queries per second. Assuming roughly 1.5 KB of index memory per vector after quantization, the dataset requires about 90 GB across all replicas. Using 4 shards with 2 replicas yields 8 shard replicas of about 11 GB each, which can be spread across four nodes with 32 GB of memory apiece.

> **Warning:** Setting `replicas: 1` in production removes failover. A single node failure makes the affected shard unavailable until it is restored from snapshot, and writes to that shard fail under `quorum` or `all` consistency.

## Summary

Decide shard count from projected growth, use `quorum` writes and `spread` placement by default, and validate sizing with a load test before launch.

title: Tuning, Monitoring, and Operational Health
body:
# Tuning, Monitoring, and Operational Health

This final section covers the operational practices needed to keep a VectorForge deployment performing well over time. It describes the key metrics, alert thresholds, and routine maintenance tasks that complement the configuration choices described in earlier sections.

## Key Metrics

The engine exposes metrics on the `/metrics` endpoint in Prometheus format. The most important are:

| Metric | Meaning | Suggested alert |
|---|---|---|
| `vf_query_latency_p99_ms` | 99th percentile query latency | Above SLO for 5 minutes |
| `vf_index_memory_bytes` | Resident index memory | Above 85 percent of node memory |
| `vf_ingest_lag_seconds` | Delay between write and searchability | Above 30 seconds |
| `vf_replica_divergence` | Records differing between replicas | Above 0 for 10 minutes |
| `vf_recall_sample` | Periodic recall estimate from shadow queries | Below configured floor |

The `vf_recall_sample` metric deserves special attention. Latency and memory can be monitored with generic tools, but recall degradation is invisible without a dedicated check.

## Enabling Shadow Recall Checks

```yaml
monitoring:
  recall_sampling:
    enabled: true
    rate: 0.001
    baseline: exact
    alert_below: 0.92
```

The engine runs a small fraction of live queries against an exact brute-force baseline and reports the overlap. Keep the sampling rate low to limit cost.

## Tuning Query Latency

When p99 latency exceeds target, work through these steps in order:

1. Confirm that the filter strategy matches the data selectivity.
2. Lower `ef_search` if recall has headroom above the alert floor.
3. Check whether a single shard is hot, indicating skewed key distribution.
4. Increase replica count for read-heavy shards.

## Snapshots and Recovery

Schedule regular snapshots. A snapshot captures the index, metadata, and configuration for a collection.

```
vforge snapshot create --collection product_catalog --label nightly
```

Test restoration quarterly on a non-production cluster. An untested backup is not a recovery plan.

## Maintenance Windows

Compaction merges index segments and removes deleted records. It is CPU and I/O intensive, so schedule it during low-traffic periods:

```yaml
maintenance:
  compaction:
    schedule: '0 3 * * 1'
    max_io_mbps: 200
```

> **Warning:** Deleting a collection is immediate and irreversible unless a snapshot exists. The `vforge collection delete` command requires the `--confirm` flag, but automation scripts sometimes pass it by habit. Restrict delete permissions to a dedicated service role and require a recent snapshot in your change process.

## Upgrade Procedure

Upgrade one node at a time. Confirm that replica divergence is zero and that recall samples are within range before proceeding to the next node. Rolling back is supported only within the same minor version.

## Final Checklist

- Alerts configured for latency, memory, ingest lag, divergence, and recall.
- Snapshots scheduled and restoration tested this quarter.
- Compaction scheduled outside peak hours.
- Model revision and metric recorded in the team's configuration repository.

title: Security & Access Control Overview
body:
## Overview

Vaultline's security model combines two complementary mechanisms. **API keys** identify calling applications, and **role-based access control (RBAC)** determines what an authenticated principal may do. This page describes how these pieces fit together and where to begin.

## Principals

Every request to the Vaultline API is made on behalf of a *principal*. There are three principal types:

- **Users** authenticate through single sign-on and act via the console or CLI.
- **Service accounts** represent automated workloads such as CI pipelines and background jobs.
- **API keys** are long-lived credentials bound to a service account or user.

## Request Evaluation

For each request, the gateway performs these steps in order:

1. Validate the credential, including signature, expiry, and revocation status.
2. Resolve the principal and its active role bindings.
3. Evaluate the requested action against the permissions granted by those roles.
4. Apply resource-level conditions such as IP allowlists.
5. Write an audit event, regardless of outcome.

If any step fails, the gateway returns **401 Unauthorized** for credential problems or **403 Forbidden** for authorization failures.

## Default Posture

New organizations start with a deny-by-default posture. No principal can read or modify resources until a role binding grants access. This behavior cannot be disabled.

## Checking Your Access

Use the CLI to confirm what the current identity can do:

```bash
vaultline auth whoami
vaultline auth can-i read:projects --project prod-eu
```

The second command prints `allowed` or `denied` along with the binding that produced the decision.

> **Note:** Access decisions are evaluated at request time. Changes to role bindings take effect within about 30 seconds across all regions.

> **Warning:** Never embed API keys in client-side code, mobile applications, or public repositories. Treat any exposed key as compromised and rotate it immediately. See the Rotating and Revoking Keys guide for the full procedure.

## Next Steps

Continue with the API Key Lifecycle guide to issue your first credential, then review the RBAC sections to scope its permissions.

title: API Key Lifecycle: Issuing Keys
body:
## Overview

An API key is a bearer credential bound to exactly one principal. This guide covers creating keys, choosing expiry windows, and storing secrets safely. Keys are issued from the console or with the CLI.

## Prerequisites

You need the `keys:create` permission in the target project. Service accounts must already exist. If you have not created one, run:

```bash
vaultline serviceaccount create svc-deploy --project prod-eu
```

## Creating a Key

Create a key with a descriptive name, a bound service account, and an expiry period:

```bash
vaultline keys create --name ci-deploy --service-account svc-deploy --expires-in 90d
```

The command returns a key identifier and a secret. The identifier (for example `key_8f2a`) is safe to log. The secret begins with `vlk_` and is used as the bearer token.

## Expiry Guidelines

Choose the shortest expiry that your automation can tolerate:

- Interactive tooling: 30 days
- CI and deployment pipelines: 90 days
- Long-running integrations: 180 days, paired with a scheduled rotation

Keys cannot exceed 365 days. Organizations may set a shorter maximum through the policy settings.

## Using the Key

Pass the secret in the `Authorization` header:

```bash
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer vlk_example_secret' https://api.vaultline.example/v2/projects
```

Requests that omit the header receive a 401 response with a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge.

## Storing Secrets

Store the secret in a dedicated secrets manager or your CI platform's encrypted variable store. Do not write it to configuration files committed to version control, and do not print it to build logs.

> **Warning:** The full secret is displayed only once, at creation time. Vaultline stores only a salted hash afterward. If the secret is lost, you must create a new key and revoke the old one.

> **Note:** Each organization may hold up to 50 active keys per service account. Revoked and expired keys do not count toward this limit.

## Listing Keys

Review existing keys and their last-used timestamps:

```bash
vaultline keys list --service-account svc-deploy
```

Keys with no recorded usage in 60 days are flagged in the console as candidates for removal.

title: Rotating and Revoking API Keys
body:
## Overview

Rotation replaces a working key with a new one without interrupting the workload that depends on it. Revocation permanently disables a key. This guide describes both procedures and when to use each.

## When to Rotate

Rotate keys on a regular schedule, when a team member with access leaves the organization, or after a key appears in logs, a ticket, or a public location. Scheduled rotation should occur at least once per expiry window.

## Zero-Downtime Rotation

Vaultline supports overlapping keys through a grace period. During this window, both the old and new keys are valid.

1. Create a replacement key for the same service account.
2. Deploy the new secret to all consumers.
3. Confirm that the old key's usage has dropped to zero.
4. Revoke the old key.

To automate steps 1 and 4 with a grace period, run:

```bash
vaultline keys rotate key_8f2a --grace-period 24h
```

The old key remains valid for 24 hours and then revokes automatically. The command returns the new key identifier and secret.

## Verifying Usage

Before revoking, check whether the old key still receives traffic:

```bash
vaultline keys usage key_8f2a --window 1h
```

The output lists request counts by endpoint and source IP. Any unexpected source indicates a consumer you have not yet migrated.

## Revocation

To revoke a key immediately, for example after suspected exposure:

```bash
vaultline keys revoke key_8f2a --reason compromised
```

Revocation takes effect within seconds. Requests using the key receive a 401 response with error code `key_revoked`. The reason is recorded in the audit log.

## Incident Response Checklist

- Revoke the exposed key.
- Review audit events for that key over the exposure window.
- Rotate any secrets the key could have been used to read.
- Notify the owning team and record the incident.

> **Warning:** Revocation cannot be undone. Any integration still using the key will fail immediately. Confirm usage with the command above before revoking a key that is not known to be compromised.

> **Note:** Rotation creates a new key with a fresh expiry window. It does not extend the lifetime of the original key, and the old key's audit history remains accessible.

## Scheduling

The `keys rotate` command accepts a `--schedule` flag with a cron expression. Scheduled rotations appear in the console under Keys, Automation.

title: RBAC Concepts: Roles, Permissions, and Bindings
body:
## Overview

Vaultline's RBAC model answers one question: which principals may perform which actions on which resources. It is built from three elements: permissions, roles, and bindings. Understanding these elements is required before you write custom policies.

## Permissions

A permission is a string in the form `resource:action`. Examples include `projects:read`, `deployments:write`, and `secrets:rotate`. Vaultline defines more than 120 permissions across 18 resource types. The full list is available with `vaultline permissions list`.

## Roles

A role is a named collection of permissions. Vaultline ships four built-in roles:

| Role | Intended use | Summary |
|---|---|---|
| Viewer | Auditors, stakeholders | Read-only access to projects and logs |
| Developer | Application engineers | Deploy and read configuration |
| Operator | SRE and platform teams | Manage infrastructure and rotate keys |
| Admin | Organization owners | Full control, including billing and roles |

Built-in roles cannot be edited. To change what a role grants, create a custom role as described in the Defining Custom Roles guide.

## Bindings

A binding attaches a role to a principal at a specific scope. Scopes are hierarchical:

- **Organization** applies to every project.
- **Project** applies to one project and its environments.
- **Environment** applies to a single environment, such as `prod-eu`.

A binding at a broader scope is inherited by narrower scopes. A binding at `prod-eu` does not grant access to `staging`.

## Evaluation Rules

When a principal holds several bindings, Vaultline computes the union of their permissions. Permissions are additive. An explicit `deny` statement, available in custom roles, overrides any allow from any binding.

```bash
vaultline bindings create --principal svc-deploy --role developer --scope project:checkout
```

## Viewing Effective Permissions

To see the full set of permissions a principal holds at a given scope:

```bash
vaultline auth effective --principal svc-deploy --scope environment:prod-eu
```

> **Note:** Effective permissions are computed at query time. They reflect inherited bindings and deny rules, so they may differ from the bindings listed directly on the principal.

> **Warning:** Granting the Admin role to a service account gives that account the ability to modify roles and bindings, including its own. Reserve Admin bindings for named human users and enforce multi-factor authentication for them.

## Best Practices

Prefer the narrowest built-in role that fits. Bind at the most specific scope possible, and review bindings quarterly.

title: Defining Custom Roles
body:
## Overview

Custom roles let you grant exactly the permissions a workload requires. They are defined as declarative manifests in YAML, stored in version control, and applied with the CLI. This guide walks through writing, testing, and applying a role.

## Role Manifest Structure

A role manifest contains metadata, a scope, and a list of permissions. The following example defines a role that can read invoices and usage data but cannot modify anything:

```yaml
apiVersion: access/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: billing-reader
  description: Read-only access to billing data
spec:
  scope: project
  permissions:
    - invoices:read
    - usage:read
    - projects:read
```

The `scope` field limits where the role may be bound. Valid values are `organization`, `project`, and `environment`.

## Applying the Role

Validate the manifest before applying it:

```bash
vaultline roles validate -f billing-reader.yaml
vaultline roles apply -f billing-reader.yaml
```

Validation checks syntax, confirms each permission exists, and reports any scope conflicts. Apply is idempotent, so running it again with no changes has no effect.

## Adding Deny Rules

Deny rules take precedence over allow rules from any binding. Use them to carve exceptions out of a broader role:

```yaml
spec:
  scope: project
  permissions:
    - secrets:read
  deny:
    - secrets:read:production
```

This allows reading secrets in general but blocks production secrets for any principal holding the role.

## Testing Before Binding

Simulate the role against a sample request before attaching it to a real principal:

```bash
vaultline roles simulate billing-reader --action invoices:read --project checkout
```

The simulator returns `allowed` or `denied` and lists the rule that matched.

> **Warning:** Avoid wildcard permissions such as `*:*` or `projects:*` in custom roles. A wildcard silently grants permissions added in future releases. List each permission explicitly so that new capabilities require a deliberate review.

> **Note:** Role names must be unique within an organization and may contain lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens. Renaming a role requires creating a new one and migrating bindings, because names are used as identifiers in the audit log.

## Versioning Roles

Keep manifests in the same repository as your infrastructure code and require review for changes. Each applied change creates a new revision that can be restored with `vaultline roles rollback billing-reader --revision 3`.

title: Scoping API Keys and IP Allowlists
body:
## Overview

Even a valid API key can be misused if it leaks. Scoping limits what a key can do, and IP allowlists limit where it can be used from. Together they reduce the damage an exposed credential can cause. This guide explains both controls.

## Permission Scoping

API keys inherit the permissions of their service account, but you can narrow them further. When creating a key, supply a permission set that is a subset of the account's permissions:

```bash
vaultline keys create --name reporting-read --service-account svc-reports --permissions usage:read,invoices:read --expires-in 180d
```

Requests that exceed the key's permission set receive a 403 response, even if the service account itself has broader access.

## Resource Scoping

Keys can also be restricted to specific projects or environments. This prevents a key issued for staging from being used against production:

```bash
vaultline keys update key_3c9d --scope environment:staging
```

## IP Allowlists

An allowlist restricts requests to a set of CIDR ranges. Requests from any other address are rejected before authorization is evaluated.

```bash
vaultline keys update key_8f2a --allow-cidr 203.0.113.0/24 --allow-cidr 198.51.100.7/32
```

Allowlists accept IPv4 and IPv6 ranges. A key with no allowlist accepts traffic from any address, so set one for every production key where the source network is known.

## Client Address Resolution

When Vaultline sits behind a load balancer, the client address comes from the `X-Forwarded-For` header. Vaultline trusts this header only from the proxy addresses configured in your organization's network settings. Requests with forged headers from untrusted sources are evaluated against the connecting address.

## Verifying a Restriction

Test an allowlist from an address outside the range. The expected response is a 403 with error code `source_not_allowed`.

> **Warning:** Do not allowlist `0.0.0.0/0` or `::/0`. That range matches every address and provides no protection. If a dynamic source address makes allowlisting difficult, consider a private network endpoint instead.

> **Note:** Allowlist changes take effect within about 30 seconds. Existing connections are not terminated, but new requests are evaluated immediately against the updated list.

## Recommended Pattern

Combine a narrow permission set, an environment scope, and an allowlist for every production key. Review these settings whenever a consumer changes networks or hosting providers.

title: Audit Logging and Access Review
body:
## Overview

Vaultline records an audit event for every authentication and authorization decision, including denied requests. Audit data supports incident investigation, compliance reporting, and periodic access reviews. This guide describes the event format and common queries.

## Event Format

Each event contains the following fields:

```yaml
timestamp: 2024-05-14T09:21:07Z
event: authz.decision
principal: svc-deploy
credential: key_8f2a
action: deployments:write
resource: environment:prod-eu
outcome: denied
reason: missing_permission
source_ip: 203.0.113.42
request_id: req_77b1e0
```

Event types include `auth.login`, `auth.failure`, `key.created`, `key.revoked`, `role.changed`, and `authz.decision`. Secret values are never logged. Only key identifiers appear.

## Querying Events

Retrieve recent denied requests for a service account:

```bash
vaultline audit query --since 1h --outcome denied --actor svc-deploy
```

Results can be exported as JSON Lines for ingestion into a SIEM:

```bash
vaultline audit export --since 7d --format jsonl --output audit-week.jsonl
```

## Access Reviews

A quarterly access review confirms that each principal still needs its bindings. A practical process:

1. Export all active bindings with `vaultline bindings list --format csv`.
2. Pull last-used data for each principal over the review period.
3. Remove bindings with no activity for 90 days.
4. Downgrade any Admin binding held by a service account.
5. Record the review and its approver.

## Alerting

Configure alerts for high-signal events, such as repeated `auth.failure` events from a single source, `key.created` for keys with Admin permissions, and any `role.changed` outside a change window.

> **Warning:** Audit events identify principals and keys by their identifiers. Restrict access to audit exports, because they reveal organizational structure and usage patterns even though they contain no secrets.

> **Note:** Audit events are retained for 400 days on the Enterprise plan and 90 days on the Standard plan. Export data you need for longer retention before it expires.

## Tamper Evidence

Events are chained with a hash of the previous event within each partition. Run `vaultline audit verify --since 30d` to confirm the chain is intact before relying on exported data in an investigation.

title: Troubleshooting 403 Errors and Least-Privilege Hardening
body:
## Overview

Authorization failures are the most common access issue reported by integrators. This guide explains how to diagnose a 403 response and how to tighten access over time so that permissions match what workloads actually use.

## Interpreting the Error

A 403 response includes a JSON body with an `error` code and a `missing` field. Common codes include:

- `missing_permission`: the principal lacks the required permission at the requested scope.
- `out_of_scope`: the binding exists but applies to a different project or environment.
- `source_not_allowed`: the key's IP allowlist rejected the source address.
- `explicit_deny`: a deny rule matched the request.

## Diagnosing the Failure

Use the explain command with the same principal, action, and scope as the failing request:

```bash
vaultline auth explain --principal svc-deploy --action deployments:write --project checkout --environment prod-eu
```

The output walks through each evaluation step and names the rule that produced the decision. In most cases, the fix is adding a binding at the correct scope or correcting a typo in the environment name.

## Least-Privilege Review

Once access works, reduce it to what is needed. Start by identifying unused permissions:

```bash
vaultline auth unused --principal svc-deploy --window 90d
```

This command lists permissions granted but not exercised during the window. Remove them by replacing the binding with a narrower custom role.

## Hardening Checklist

- Replace Admin and Operator bindings on service accounts with custom roles.
- Set an IP allowlist on every production key.
- Scope each key to a single environment.
- Set expiry on every key, with rotation scheduled before it lapses.
- Enable alerts for repeated 403 responses from one principal, which may indicate misconfiguration or probing.

> **Warning:** Do not respond to a 403 by granting the Admin role. This resolves the immediate error but permanently widens the blast radius of the credential. Identify the missing permission and grant only that.

> **Note:** The explain command reflects current bindings. If a change was made recently, allow about 30 seconds for propagation before concluding that the fix has not worked.

## Escalation

If `auth explain` shows a decision that does not match your bindings, contact support with the `request_id` from the failing response. Include the output of the explain command, but never include the key secret.

title: Connection Pool Exhaustion
body:
# Connection Pool Exhaustion

This page describes how to diagnose and resolve situations where the Tessera Data Gateway reports `POOL_EXHAUSTED` errors or where client requests queue for extended periods before acquiring a connection.

## Symptoms

- Clients receive `503 Service Unavailable` with the body `pool wait timeout exceeded`.
- The `pool.active` metric remains at or near `pool.max_size` for sustained intervals.
- Latency percentiles (p95 and p99) rise sharply while CPU and memory usage remain normal.

## Root Causes

Exhaustion usually falls into one of three categories:

1. **Undersized pool.** The configured `max_size` is lower than peak concurrent demand.
2. **Connection leaks.** Application code acquires connections but does not release them, often in error paths.
3. **Slow upstream queries.** Connections are held open while long-running queries complete, reducing effective capacity.

## Diagnostic Steps

Start by inspecting the live pool state:

```bash
tessera-cli pool stats --pool primary --watch 5s
```

Compare `acquired_total` against `released_total`. A growing gap over time strongly suggests a leak. Next, identify the longest-held connections:

```bash
tessera-cli pool holders --pool primary --sort held_for --limit 10
```

## Resolution

For an undersized pool, increase the limit in your configuration file:

```yaml
pool:
  primary:
    max_size: 64
    min_idle: 8
    acquire_timeout: 2s
    max_lifetime: 30m
    idle_timeout: 5m
```

Set `acquire_timeout` deliberately. A value that is too long hides the problem by making clients wait, while a value that is too short causes avoidable failures during brief spikes.

For leaks, ensure every acquisition is paired with a release, preferably through a scoped construct such as a `try-with-resources` block or a `defer` statement.

> **Warning:** Raising `max_size` without addressing leaks only delays the failure. Each connection holds server-side memory, and the upstream database may enforce its own connection ceiling. Verify the database limit before increasing the gateway pool.

## Verification

After changes, confirm that `pool.wait_ms_p99` returns below 50 ms under normal load and that `pool.active` peaks below 80 percent of `max_size` during your busiest hour. Record results in your change log so future regressions can be compared against a known baseline.

title: Memory Pressure and Heap Sizing
body:
# Memory Pressure and Heap Sizing

Tessera Data Gateway runs on the managed runtime and allocates memory for query buffers, result sets, and the in-process cache. This page explains how to recognize memory pressure and how to size the heap appropriately.

## Symptoms

- Garbage collection pauses exceeding 500 ms appear in the gateway log.
- The process is terminated by the operating system with an out-of-memory signal.
- Throughput degrades gradually over hours and recovers after a restart.

## Understanding the Memory Budget

The gateway divides memory into four regions:

| Region | Purpose | Default share |
|---|---|---|
| Heap | Objects, buffers, sessions | 60 percent |
| Cache | Result and metadata cache | 25 percent |
| Direct | Network and file I/O buffers | 10 percent |
| Reserve | Headroom for spikes | 5 percent |

The shares are applied to `memory.limit`, which defaults to 80 percent of the container or host memory.

## Diagnostic Commands

Capture a memory summary during a period of degradation:

```bash
tessera-cli memory report --format table
```

If heap usage stays above 85 percent after a full collection cycle, the working set exceeds the heap. Generate a heap histogram to identify the dominant object types:

```bash
tessera-cli heap histogram --top 15
```

## Sizing Guidance

Adjust the heap in the runtime section of your configuration:

```yaml
memory:
  limit: 12GiB
  heap_fraction: 0.6
  cache_fraction: 0.2
  gc:
    pause_target: 200ms
    concurrent_threads: 4
```

Reduce `cache_fraction` before increasing the overall limit if the cache is not improving hit ratio. A cache that is larger than its useful working set consumes memory without benefit.

> **Note:** Container orchestrators count the total process footprint, including direct buffers and native allocations. A `limit` that equals the container memory will almost always be killed. Leave at least 15 percent of container memory unallocated to the gateway configuration.

> **Warning:** Do not disable garbage collection logging to reduce overhead. The GC log is the primary evidence for distinguishing a true leak from a sizing problem, and it is required when filing a support request.

## Checklist

1. Confirm the container limit exceeds `memory.limit` by at least 15 percent.
2. Verify GC pauses stay below `pause_target` at p99.
3. Watch the heap after a full collection. A steadily rising floor indicates a leak rather than undersizing.

If the floor rises without a corresponding increase in traffic, collect a diagnostic bundle (see the Log Analysis page) and open a ticket.

title: Slow Query Diagnosis with EXPLAIN Plans
body:
# Slow Query Diagnosis with EXPLAIN Plans

When a query routed through the gateway exceeds its latency target, the execution plan is the first artifact to examine. This page covers how to request, read, and act on plans produced by the gateway planner.

## Capturing a Plan

Prefix any statement with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to execute it and record actual timings alongside estimates:

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT o.order_id, c.region, SUM(o.total)
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'
GROUP BY o.order_id, c.region;
```

Use plain `EXPLAIN` when the query must not run, for example against production write paths.

## Reading the Output

Each plan node reports two numbers that matter most:

- **Estimated rows** versus **actual rows.** A discrepancy greater than tenfold indicates stale statistics or a predicate the planner cannot model.
- **Actual time** on each node, reported as startup and total milliseconds. The node with the largest self-time, not the largest cumulative time, is the usual bottleneck.

## Common Patterns

**Sequential scan on a large table.** The planner chose a full scan because no index matches the predicate, or because statistics suggest most rows qualify. Check whether the filter is sargable. Wrapping an indexed column in a function, such as `date(created_at)`, prevents index use.

**Nested loop with a high loop count.** Inner-side work repeats once per outer row. Confirm statistics with:

```sql
ANALYZE orders;
ANALYZE customers;
```

**Sort spilling to disk.** The `Sort Method: external merge` line means `work_mem` was insufficient. Raise it for the session rather than globally:

```sql
SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB';
```

## Forcing Plan Changes

The gateway supports plan hints through the `/*+ */` comment syntax. Use them only after confirming the root cause:

```sql
SELECT /*+ INDEX(o idx_orders_created) */ o.order_id
FROM orders o
WHERE o.created_at >= now() - interval '7 days';
```

> **Warning:** Hints freeze a plan shape. When data distribution changes, a hinted query can become slower than the planner's choice. Review hinted queries quarterly and remove hints that no longer provide benefit.

> **Note:** `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes the statement, including any side effects. Wrap data-modifying statements in a transaction and roll back afterward.

## Verification

Re-run the plan after each change and record the total execution time. Compare p95 latency over at least 24 hours of traffic, since a single timed run can mislead when caches are cold.

title: Index Fragmentation and Rebuild Scheduling
body:
# Index Fragmentation and Rebuild Scheduling

Indexes in the gateway's embedded storage engine fragment over time as rows are updated and deleted. Fragmented indexes read more pages per lookup, which increases I/O and lengthens query latency. This page explains how to measure fragmentation and schedule rebuilds without disrupting traffic.

## Measuring Fragmentation

The `index inspect` command reports page density and fragmentation ratio for each index:

```bash
tessera-cli index inspect --table orders --all
```

The key columns are:

- `fill_factor`: the average proportion of each page holding live data. Values below 0.6 indicate sparse pages.
- `frag_ratio`: the proportion of logically adjacent pages that are not physically adjacent. Values above 0.3 typically justify a rebuild.
- `dead_entries`: index entries pointing to deleted rows awaiting cleanup.

## When Fragmentation Matters

Fragmentation affects read-heavy indexes most. Write-heavy append-only indexes, such as time-series keys, rarely fragment significantly. Prioritize rebuilds for indexes that serve point lookups and range scans on frequently updated columns.

## Scheduling a Rebuild

Rebuilds take a short exclusive lock on the index metadata and then build a replacement in the background. Schedule them during low-traffic windows:

```yaml
maintenance:
  index_rebuild:
    enabled: true
    schedule: '0 2 * * 0'
    thresholds:
      frag_ratio: 0.3
      fill_factor_below: 0.6
    max_concurrent: 1
    io_limit_mbps: 40
```

The `io_limit_mbps` setting prevents the rebuild from competing with foreground queries. Lower it on shared storage. Raise it only on dedicated volumes with measured headroom.

To trigger a rebuild manually:

```bash
tessera-cli index rebuild --table orders --name idx_orders_customer --online
```

The `--online` flag keeps the index readable during the rebuild.

> **Warning:** Running a rebuild without `--online` blocks writes to the table until completion. On tables above 100 million rows this can exceed the default write timeout and cause client errors. Always use `--online` in production.

> **Note:** A rebuild temporarily requires roughly twice the index's disk footprint. Confirm free space before starting, or the rebuild aborts and leaves the original index intact.

## Verifying the Result

After the rebuild completes, rerun `index inspect` and confirm `frag_ratio` has dropped below 0.1. Compare p95 latency for the affected query patterns against the pre-rebuild baseline. If latency did not improve, fragmentation was not the bottleneck, and the EXPLAIN plan should be reviewed instead.

title: Network Timeouts and Retry Backoff
body:
# Network Timeouts and Retry Backoff

The gateway communicates with upstream services over pooled HTTP/2 and binary protocol connections. Misconfigured timeouts are a frequent source of cascading failures, because a slow dependency can hold threads and connections until the entire service stalls. This page describes the timeout hierarchy and how to tune retry behavior safely.

## Timeout Hierarchy

Every outbound request is governed by four timers, evaluated in order:

1. **Connect timeout**: maximum time to establish a TCP and TLS session.
2. **Write timeout**: maximum time to send the request body.
3. **Read timeout**: maximum time between received bytes.
4. **Request deadline**: maximum total elapsed time, including retries.

The request deadline should always be the largest value that a client can tolerate. Individual attempts should be shorter so that retries can occur within the deadline.

## Symptoms of Misconfiguration

- Errors labeled `upstream deadline exceeded` appear in bursts that coincide with brief upstream slowdowns.
- Retry counts climb while success rates fall, indicating that retries amplify load.
- Connection counts spike during incidents, then drop sharply when timeouts fire.

## Recommended Configuration

```yaml
upstream:
  orders_service:
    connect_timeout: 500ms
    read_timeout: 2s
    request_deadline: 5s
    retry:
      max_attempts: 3
      backoff: exponential
      base_delay: 100ms
      max_delay: 1s
      jitter: full
      retry_on: [connect_error, unavailable]
```

Full jitter spreads retries across time, preventing synchronized waves of traffic from overwhelming a recovering service. Restrict `retry_on` to idempotent failure classes. Retrying a timeout on a non-idempotent write can produce duplicate records.

## Circuit Breaking

When the error rate for an upstream exceeds `breaker.failure_threshold` within the sliding window, the gateway fails requests immediately for `breaker.open_duration`. This protects both the gateway and the upstream. Monitor the `breaker.state` metric, and treat frequent transitions as a signal to revisit capacity rather than as normal behavior.

```bash
tessera-cli upstream status --name orders_service --show breaker,retries
```

> **Warning:** Retries multiply load. With three attempts and a failing upstream, traffic can increase to three times the normal rate at the moment the upstream is least able to handle it. Always pair retries with a circuit breaker and a retry budget, typically no more than 10 percent of total requests.

> **Note:** Version 4.0.8 measures the request deadline from the moment the request enters the gateway queue, not from dispatch. Queue wait time therefore counts against the deadline.

## Verification

Use a fault injection test to delay the upstream by a known amount, then confirm that requests fail within `request_deadline` plus a small margin, and that the retry count never exceeds `max_attempts`.

title: Batch Ingestion Throughput Tuning
body:
# Batch Ingestion Throughput Tuning

Batch ingestion moves large volumes of records into the gateway from files, message queues, or external exports. Throughput depends on batch size, parallelism, and how the gateway commits data. This page explains how to find the limiting factor and tune the pipeline accordingly.

## Establishing a Baseline

Before changing any setting, measure current throughput with the built-in benchmark mode:

```bash
tessera-cli ingest bench --source ./sample/orders.csv --dry-run --report
```

The report separates time spent parsing, validating, and committing. The largest share identifies the stage to optimize.

## Batch Size

Larger batches amortize per-commit overhead but increase memory use and the cost of retrying a failed batch. A practical starting range is 5,000 to 20,000 rows. Configure it in the pipeline definition:

```yaml
ingest:
  pipeline: orders_daily
  batch:
    max_rows: 10000
    max_bytes: 32MiB
    flush_interval: 2s
  parallelism:
    parsers: 4
    writers: 2
  commit:
    mode: async
    durability: group
```

The batch flushes at whichever limit is reached first, so `flush_interval` ensures slow sources still make progress.

## Parallelism

Parsers are CPU-bound and should generally not exceed the number of physical cores available to the gateway. Writers are I/O-bound and benefit from more concurrency, up to the point where the storage engine's write queue saturates. Watch the `ingest.writer_queue_depth` metric. A queue that stays above 80 percent of capacity means writers are the bottleneck.

## Commit Durability

The `durability` setting controls how often data is flushed to disk:

- `per_batch`: every batch is fsynced before acknowledgment. Safest, slowest.
- `group`: fsyncs are coalesced across concurrent writers. Recommended for most workloads.
- `relaxed`: acknowledgments precede fsync. Fastest, with a window of possible loss on crash.

> **Warning:** The `relaxed` mode can lose the most recent acknowledged batches if the host loses power. Use it only for re-derivable data such as staging copies or caches.

## Validation Overhead

Schema validation can consume a large share of CPU on wide records. If the source is trusted, reduce validation to structural checks:

```bash
tessera-cli ingest run --pipeline orders_daily --validate structural
```

> **Note:** Structural validation skips type coercion checks. Malformed values will be written as null rather than rejected. Schedule a periodic full validation run to catch drift.

## Verification

Rerun the benchmark with identical input and compare rows per second. Record the new configuration alongside the result so that future changes can be evaluated against a documented baseline.

title: Cache Eviction and Hit Ratio
body:
# Cache Eviction and Hit Ratio

The gateway maintains an in-process cache for query results and metadata lookups. A high hit ratio reduces load on upstream databases; a low one wastes memory without benefit. This page covers how to interpret cache metrics and select an eviction policy suited to your workload.

## Key Metrics

- `cache.hit_ratio`: hits divided by total lookups over a rolling window.
- `cache.evictions_per_sec`: the rate at which entries are removed to make room.
- `cache.bytes_used` and `cache.entries`: current footprint.
- `cache.avg_entry_age`: the mean time since an entry was last written.

A hit ratio below 0.5 with a high eviction rate suggests the working set exceeds capacity. A high hit ratio with few evictions suggests the cache may be larger than necessary.

## Eviction Policies

The gateway supports three policies:

| Policy | Behavior | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| `lru` | Evicts least recently used | Recency-driven access patterns |
| `lfu` | Evicts least frequently used | Stable hot sets with occasional scans |
| `tinylfu` | Admits entries based on frequency sketch | Mixed workloads with scan pressure |

The `tinylfu` policy is the default in 4.1.0 because it resists cache pollution from one-time full table reads.

## Configuration

```yaml
cache:
  enabled: true
  max_bytes: 2GiB
  policy: tinylfu
  default_ttl: 300s
  per_route:
    catalog_lookup:
      ttl: 3600s
      max_bytes: 256MiB
    order_summary:
      ttl: 30s
      bypass_when: 'request.header.x-no-cache == true'
```

Separate TTLs by data volatility. Reference data such as product catalogs can tolerate long lifetimes, while order summaries should expire quickly.

## Diagnosing Low Hit Ratio

First check whether requests are cacheable at all. Queries containing non-deterministic functions, such as `now()`, produce a different cache key on every call. Inspect key distribution:

```bash
tessera-cli cache keys --top 20 --show hits,misses
```

Keys with many misses and a single occurrence are candidates for exclusion from caching.

> **Warning:** Long TTLs on mutable data serve stale results. Before raising `ttl` to improve hit ratio, confirm that the downstream consumers accept the staleness window in writing, and document the decision in the route configuration.

> **Note:** Changing `policy` clears the cache. Schedule policy changes during maintenance windows to avoid a temporary spike in upstream load.

## Verification

After tuning, monitor `cache.hit_ratio` for at least one full traffic cycle, including peak periods. Confirm that `cache.bytes_used` remains below `max_bytes` with margin, and that upstream query rate fell by a proportion consistent with the new hit ratio.

title: Log Analysis and Diagnostic Bundles
body:
# Log Analysis and Diagnostic Bundles

When an incident cannot be resolved from metrics alone, the gateway's structured logs and diagnostic bundles provide the detail needed for root cause analysis. This page describes log levels, how to filter entries efficiently, and how to produce a bundle suitable for support.

## Log Structure

Every entry is written as a single JSON line with consistent fields:

```json
{"ts":"2024-05-14T09:21:07.418Z","level":"WARN","component":"pool","request_id":"r-7f3a91","msg":"acquire wait exceeded","wait_ms":2104}
```

The fields `request_id` and `trace_id` allow you to follow a single request across components. Include `request_id` in any support correspondence.

## Log Levels

- `ERROR`: an operation failed and the client received an error.
- `WARN`: an operation succeeded but exceeded a threshold, or a fallback was used.
- `INFO`: lifecycle events such as startup, configuration reloads, and certificate rotation.
- `DEBUG`: detailed internal state. Generates significant volume and should be enabled only for short periods.

## Filtering Logs

Use the CLI to extract relevant entries without parsing the raw files manually:

```bash
tessera-cli logs tail --component pool --level WARN,ERROR --since 30m
```

To follow a specific request across all components:

```bash
tessera-cli logs trace --request-id r-7f3a91
```

## Adjusting Verbosity at Runtime

Raise the level for a single component without restarting the gateway:

```bash
tessera-cli logs level --component planner --set DEBUG --ttl 15m
```

The `--ttl` flag reverts the level automatically, which prevents forgotten debug settings from filling disks.

## Generating a Diagnostic Bundle

A diagnostic bundle packages recent logs, configuration with secrets redacted, metric snapshots, and thread dumps into a single archive:

```bash
tessera-cli diag bundle --since 2h --include logs,metrics,config,threads --output /var/tmp/diag
```

The bundle is typically 50 to 400 megabytes depending on log volume. Verify the checksum file accompanies the archive before transferring it.

> **Warning:** Bundles contain query text, which may include personal data. Review your organization's data handling policy before sharing a bundle externally. Use `--redact-queries` to replace literal values with placeholders.

> **Note:** Thread dumps are captured at the moment of collection. For intermittent hangs, collect two or three bundles spaced 30 seconds apart so that stuck threads can be distinguished from transient ones.

## Retention

Logs rotate daily and are retained for 14 days by default. Adjust `logging.retention_days` in the configuration file. Diagnostic bundles are not rotated automatically and must be deleted manually once no longer needed.
